e.t: Abisour, also rendered Avisur, is a personal name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Septuagint, it appears twice, both times in 1 Chronicles 2:28–29. Because the available record does not include the verse text or a broader definition, the name itself is the main meaning: it identifies a particular person in the genealogy. Its precise significance in those verses depends on the surrounding passage.

This word means “love.” As a noun, it names love as an affection or devotion between people and toward God. In the Greek Old Testament and related LXX writings, it can describe love in human relationships and in a person’s response to God or wisdom. It occurs 18 times in this LXX corpus, with especially frequent use in Song of Songs. Its precise emphasis in any verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This noun refers to ritual service—an ordered act or practice carried out as part of religious worship. It brings together the ideas of a ritual and service, describing the performance of sacred duties rather than a person or object. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 4 Maccabees 7:9. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning is ritual service.

Azael, also rendered Azel, is a personal name in the Greek Old Testament. It identifies a person rather than describing an action, quality, or object, so its ordinary meaning is the name itself, not a general concept to be translated. The name occurs 24 times in the LXX Old Testament corpus, beginning in 1 Kings 19:15 and continuing through Amos 1:4. Scripture supplies the name but does not define an additional meaning for it.

This adjective means “of a goat,” describing something connected with or belonging to a goat. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears four times, all in four verses: three in Exodus and one in Numbers. Its use includes descriptions of goat-related material or items, but the precise role in any particular verse depends on the surrounding wording. It is a specific descriptive word rather than a broad term for animals in general.

This adjective means “heard”: it describes something that can be perceived by listening or that has become audible. In the Greek Old Testament and deuterocanonical books, it occurs 23 times, so it may describe speech, sounds, or reports depending on the sentence around it. Its central idea remains simple—the thing is heard rather than merely seen or silently known. The exact force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding wording.

This Greek LXX noun means “fruit-trees,” referring to trees that bear edible fruit. It is a plural word, so it speaks of more than one such tree rather than a single plant or a particular kind of fruit. The word occurs four times in the Greek LXX corpus, appearing three times in Song of Songs and once in 1 Maccabees. Its exact force in any individual passage depends on the surrounding verse and context.

This LXX verb means “pollute”: to make something unclean or contaminated. It describes an action that spoils purity rather than preserving what is clean. The word occurs five times in the Greek Old Testament and related LXX corpus, appearing in Daniel, Malachi, and Sirach. Its exact force in any particular passage depends on what is being polluted and the surrounding context, but its central idea remains the bringing of uncleanness or corruption to something. It is a verb, so it expresses the act of polluting rather than naming the impurity itself.

This noun refers to “social disturbance; state of war”—a condition of public unrest or armed conflict. It describes disorder affecting a community rather than a person, object, or isolated action. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs twice, both times in 2 Maccabees 14, showing a focused use for serious social or political turmoil. Its exact force in either verse depends on the surrounding passage, which is not included here.

This Greek LXX verb means “cry out”—to call aloud in a strong, audible voice. It describes speech that rises above ordinary conversation, whether as a public shout, a forceful call, or an urgent vocal response. The word occurs 14 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical writings, so its basic sense is consistent across a range of passages. The surrounding verse determines whether the cry expresses urgency, command, alarm, or collective response; the word itself identifies the act of crying out aloud.

This adjective means “unlamented,” describing someone who is not mourned or lamented after death. It expresses the absence of public or personal grieving associated with a deceased person. The word appears once in the Greek LXX corpus represented here, in 2 Maccabees 5:10. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and context, but its basic meaning is that no lament is offered for the person described.

This noun refers to sending something away or getting rid of it. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at Leviticus 16:10, and describes the basic action of removal or dismissal. The word therefore focuses on something being sent away rather than kept or retained. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central meaning remains the act of sending away or getting rid of something.

This Greek LXX verb means “weak and sickly,” describing a person whose bodily condition is feeble or unwell. It presents weakness or sickness as a condition someone experiences, rather than naming a person or object. The word occurs 14 times in the Greek Old Testament and related LXX writings, with occurrences from 2 Samuel through Sirach. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea remains physical weakness or illness.

ἄσκησις means “exercise” or “practice”: deliberate training that develops ability through repeated effort. It is a noun, so it names the activity or discipline itself rather than the person who performs it. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, in 4 Maccabees 13:22. The word can therefore describe purposeful training in a broad sense. Its exact force depends on the surrounding text, which is not included here.

This Greek LXX noun means “lightning,” the bright flash seen in the sky during a storm. It names a visible natural phenomenon and may be used for lightning appearing in flashes or in multiple bolts. The word occurs 21 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books represented in this corpus, including passages from Exodus, Deuteronomy, Job, Psalms, Daniel, Jeremiah, and Sirach. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its basic meaning remains the sudden brightness of lightning.

This word describes someone or something “sprung from the land itself,” emphasizing native origin. It can function as a noun for a native person or as an adjective describing something belonging to the land from which it came. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 14 times, so it expresses a recurring idea rather than a unique name or event. Its exact force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central meaning remains rootedness in the land itself.

This word is a proper name identifying the Apharsathachaioi, also rendered Afarsathakhei. It is not presented as an ordinary descriptive word with a broader everyday meaning, but as the designation of a named people or group. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs only once, in Ezra 4:9. Its precise historical identity and role must therefore be understood from that passage and its surrounding context rather than from the name itself.

This verb means “reach”—to arrive at or come to a destination. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings, it describes reaching a place or point, rather than naming the place itself. Its ordinary sense is straightforward: someone or something comes as far as a particular location or limit. The word occurs 12 times in this Greek biblical corpus, across Genesis, Job, Proverbs, Sirach, and 2 Maccabees. Its precise force in any verse depends on what destination or limit the surrounding sentence identifies.

This word is a proper name identifying “Baalermōn,” also written “Vaalermon,” rather than describing an action, quality, or ordinary object. It functions as a personal or place name in the Greek Old Testament tradition. The word occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, at 1 Chronicles 5:23. Because no surrounding verse text is provided here, the name’s specific reference in that passage cannot be identified more precisely, but its lexical function is clear: it is a name, not a general descriptive term.

Baithachou is a proper name, also identified as “Vethakhu.” It refers to a named place or location rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, this name appears once, in Joshua 15:53. The available information identifies the name and its reference, but does not provide enough surrounding verse text to explain further details about the place or its role in that passage.

This noun refers to a military position or equipment used in warfare, especially an “artillary emplacement” or “engines of war.” It describes siege-related machinery or a prepared military installation rather than a person or action. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs six times, including passages in Jeremiah, Ezekiel, and 1 Maccabees. Its exact force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This Greek LXX noun means “curl.” It names curled hair or a curled strand, giving a simple description of its shape rather than expressing an action or quality. The word occurs twice in the Greek Old Testament portion represented here, both times in Song of Songs, where it contributes to descriptions of personal appearance. Its precise significance in either verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning remains a curl.

This word is a proper name, rendered “Bōkai” or “Voke.” It identifies a person rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs three times, all within two verses in 1 Chronicles: 5:31 and 6:36. Because it functions as a personal name, its meaning is primarily its identification of that individual, while the surrounding genealogical context supplies the details about who the person was.

This Greek word means “know.” As a verb, it describes possessing knowledge, recognizing something, or being aware of it. In the Greek Old Testament, it is used broadly across both the Old Testament and deuterocanonical books, appearing 650 times in 614 verses. Its frequent use shows that knowing is a common way Scripture speaks about awareness and understanding. The precise force of the word in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central meaning remains knowing or recognizing something.

This verb means “show”: to make something known or visible to another person. It describes the act of presenting, pointing out, or revealing something so that it can be recognized. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 115 times across 108 verses, showing that it is a broadly used word for communicating something by making it apparent. Its exact force in any particular verse depends on what is being shown and the surrounding sentence.

This verb means “succeed”: it describes one person or thing following another or taking up what comes next. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs nine times, so its basic idea is repeated across several passages rather than being limited to one setting. The surrounding verse determines exactly what or whom someone succeeds, but the word itself expresses succession or successful continuation. Its lexical meaning is “succeed,” and it functions as an action word.

This verb means “strain through” or “filter,” describing the act of passing something through a barrier so that material is separated or clarified. It presents a practical action rather than a person, object, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Job 28:1. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording, but the central idea remains the careful separation or purification of material by straining it through.

This LXX word means “assay” or “assess”: to examine something carefully in order to determine its quality, condition, or value. It can describe the testing of people, motives, or what is inward, as well as the examination of something being evaluated. The word occurs 33 times in the Greek Old Testament and deuterocanonical books, showing a recurring idea of careful testing rather than a quick or careless judgment. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding context.

This Greek LXX noun means “spear-bearer,” referring to a person whose role is to carry a spear, likely as part of an armed group. It is a specific occupational or military designation rather than a general word for a weapon or soldier. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, in 1 Chronicles 12:25. The surrounding verse text is needed to explain the person’s particular role in that passage.

This word means “subject,” referring to someone placed under another’s authority or rule. It can function as a noun for such a person or as an adjective describing one in that position. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings, it occurs 295 times, so it is a broad and recurring term rather than a rare title. Its exact force in any passage depends on the surrounding sentence and whether it describes a person, status, or relationship.

This noun means “ill-will” or “enmity”: a hostile attitude or active opposition directed toward another person or group. It describes more than a passing dislike; it points to settled hostility between parties. In the Greek Old Testament writings represented here, it occurs five times, all in 2 and 3 Maccabees. One English rendering is “enmity,” which fits the central sense. The precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the word consistently names hostility or antagonism rather than friendship or goodwill.

This noun means “aspect; shape,” referring to the visible character or form of something. It describes how something appears or is shaped, whether discussing a person, an object, or what is seen. The word occurs 50 times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented in this LXX corpus, so its basic sense is used across varied descriptions rather than limited to one subject or setting.

This noun means “freedom”: the condition of being free rather than under restraint or compulsion. It names liberty as a state or possession, and its meaning can apply to a person’s social or personal condition. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs five times, including once in Leviticus and four times in later Jewish writings. The word’s precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea remains freedom or liberty.

Eliazer is a personal name, identifying an individual rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, at 1 Chronicles 12:13. The name itself supplies the lexical meaning: “Eliazer.” Because the surrounding verse text is not included here, its specific role in that passage cannot be described further. This word functions as a proper name, so its meaning is chiefly its use as the identifying name of a person.

This Greek verb describes acting with vehement force or intense energy. It presents strong, forceful action rather than something mild, hesitant, or restrained. The word appears once in the Greek LXX corpus, in 3 Maccabees 1:28. Because the verse text and surrounding context are not included here, the word’s exact force in that sentence must be understood from its immediate setting. Its core meaning remains the idea of doing something vehemently or with powerful intensity.

This noun refers to atonement or propitiation—the making of amends for sin so that the relationship between God and his people may be restored. It names the act or provision by which wrongdoing is dealt with before God, rather than describing a person or ordinary object. In the Greek Old Testament, this word occurs once, in Numbers 29:11, and its English rendering there is “atonement.”

This Greek verb means “come up.” It describes someone or something coming upward or appearing in a higher position, while the surrounding sentence determines the precise sense. In the Greek Old Testament and related LXX writings, it occurs twice: once in 3 Maccabees and once in the Epistle of Jeremiah. Its basic idea remains simple: something comes up or emerges. [Evidence: p03:word:lxx:L705103:identity; p03:word:lxx:L705103:occurrences]

This verb means “pile up”: to place things together in a heap or gathered stack. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs four times, including three times in Leviticus 1 in descriptions of arranging sacrificial wood. Its basic sense is physical and practical—bringing separate pieces together into a pile. The surrounding passage determines exactly what is being piled up, but the word itself emphasizes the act of gathering and stacking rather than the material or purpose.

This noun refers to a small settled place—a “village” or “hamlet.” It identifies a community smaller than a town or city, rather than describing a person, action, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament (the Septuagint), it occurs one time, in 1 Chronicles 27:25. Because the word is found only once in this corpus, its broader range of use cannot be established from additional passages.

Esdriel, also rendered Ezthril, is a proper name identifying a person in the Greek Old Testament. It is not a general word describing an action, quality, or object, so its meaning is chiefly the individual’s name. This name occurs twice in the LXX, once in 1 Chronicles 5:24 and once in Nehemiah 11:13. Without the surrounding verse text, the name alone does not indicate the person’s family, role, or significance in either passage.

Esthaol is a proper name, preserved in English as “Esthaol.” It does not describe an action, quality, or relationship; it identifies a named place or person in the Greek Old Testament wording. The name occurs five times, all in Judges, from Judges 13:25 through Judges 18:11. Its exact reference is needed to determine whether the name points to a location or a person in a particular passage.

This Greek LXX word means “inside; inner.” It describes location within something or points inward, and it can function as either an adverb or a preposition. Thus, it may indicate that something is within an area or identify an inner part rather than an outside surface. The word occurs 12 times in the Greek Old Testament and related LXX corpus, including descriptions of inner parts and locations. Its exact rendering in English depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea remains what is within or toward the inside.

This Greek LXX noun expresses “character of the,” referring to the character of someone or something identified by the surrounding context. The supplied phrase is incomplete by itself, so it does not specify whose character is meant. It occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, at 2 Maccabees 6:29. The exact reference of “the” must therefore be understood from that verse and its wider passage.

This verb means “make ready” or “get ready.” It describes preparing someone or something so that it is ready for what follows. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 4 Maccabees 5:32. The word itself expresses readiness and preparation, while the surrounding verse determines what is being prepared and for what purpose. Its basic sense is active: bringing something into a suitable state of readiness.

Ephrathi, also rendered Efrathi, is a proper name referring to a person or designation rather than describing an action or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at 1 Kings 11:26. The available lexical wording gives only the name itself, so its precise reference is determined by the surrounding verse and passage. This is a Greek LXX word and should be understood within that corpus.

Zaboucham, also rendered Zavukham, is a personal name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in 1 Chronicles 5:14. The available information identifies the person by name but does not provide enough surrounding verse text to explain the individual’s role or significance. Its meaning is therefore best given as the personal name itself, with the alternate rendering preserved.

This word means “sound”—an audible noise or tone. As a noun, it refers to what is heard; as a verb, it describes producing or making a sound. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs eight times, including uses connected with ordinary noises and musical sound. Its basic meaning remains focused on audible sound rather than a particular message or speech. The surrounding verse determines what produces the sound and what significance it has there.

Thie is a proper name, rendered as “Thie.” It identifies a named individual or designation rather than describing an action, quality, or relationship. In the Greek Old Testament (LXX), this word occurs once, at 1 Chronicles 6:19. Because no verse text or surrounding context is available here, the name’s specific identity and role cannot be explained further from this word alone.

This noun refers to what is distinctive about something or what belongs to it as its property. It can describe a thing’s particular character or something that is specially its own, depending on the sentence. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, at 3 Maccabees 7:17. That reference identifies its location, but the exact force of the word there must come from the verse and its surrounding context.

Iephthamai, also rendered Iefthame, is a personal name in the Greek Old Testament. It identifies an individual rather than describing an action, quality, or object. This name occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, in Joshua 19:33. Because the available wording does not include the verse text or surrounding passage, the name’s specific identity and role cannot be explained further here. Its basic meaning is therefore its function as a proper name: a label used to identify a particular person in the biblical account.

Inael, also given as Inel, is a proper name rather than a common word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, in Joshua 19:27. The available wording identifies the name itself but does not provide a further descriptive meaning or explanation of its name elements. Its significance beyond naming depends on the surrounding passage and the person or place to which the name refers.

This word is a personal name, rendered as “Iōsephia; Iosefia.” It identifies a particular person rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament corpus, it occurs once, in Ezra 8:10. Because the available information gives the name but not the surrounding verse text, its specific role in that passage cannot be described further here. The name itself is the complete lexical meaning provided for this word.

Kamouēl; Kamoil is a personal name in the Greek Old Testament. It identifies a person rather than describing an action, quality, or object. The name occurs three times in the Greek LXX corpus, appearing once each in Genesis, Numbers, and 1 Chronicles. Its precise reference to a particular individual depends on the surrounding passage, but the word itself functions as a proper name. English spellings may preserve the name in slightly different forms, while its basic meaning here is simply the personal name Kamouēl or Kamoil.

This verb means to embolden someone—to give courage or confidence so that the person becomes bolder. It describes an action that strengthens another person’s resolve rather than merely describing an inner feeling. In the Greek LXX, it occurs once, at 2 Chronicles 32:8. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the word’s central sense is to encourage someone toward courage and confidence.

This verb means to testify against someone, giving testimony that stands as an accusation or witness against them. It describes speaking formally or publicly in opposition to another person. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs five times, so its central idea remains consistent: testimony directed against someone rather than merely speaking about them. The surrounding passage determines who is speaking and what charge or matter is being presented.

gl: betray utterly; leave in the lurch
d: betray utterly; leave in the lurch

e.t: This Greek LXX verb means to betray utterly or to leave someone in the lurch. It describes abandoning a person when loyalty or support is expected, emphasizing a serious act of betrayal rather than a minor failure. The word occurs once in the Greek Old Testament translation corpus, at 4 Maccabees 2:10. Since the surrounding verse text is not available here, its precise force in that sentence must be understood from the passage itself, but its central sense is complete betrayal or abandonment.

“Bring prosperity” is a verb describing the act of causing someone or something to prosper, succeed, or flourish. It presents prosperity as something being brought about rather than merely possessed. In the Greek Septuagint corpus, this word occurs six times, across Psalms, Proverbs, and 1 Maccabees. Its exact force in any particular verse depends on what or whom it describes, but its central idea remains the granting or producing of favorable progress and well-being.

This Greek LXX noun means “potter”: a person who forms clay into pottery or other earthen vessels. It refers to the craftsperson rather than to the vessel being made. The word occurs 16 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books represented here, especially in Isaiah and Jeremiah. Its appearances include references to a potter, a potter’s work, or something belonging to a potter, while its central meaning remains the same throughout this corpus.

To flatter means to praise or speak favorably toward someone in a way intended to please them, often without honest simplicity. This word is a verb, so it describes the act of flattering rather than a person or quality. It occurs twice in the Greek LXX corpus, once in Job and once in Wisdom, showing the same basic action across both writings. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and context.

This word means “goblet,” referring to a drinking vessel. It is a noun used for a special or valuable cup, rather than for drinking in general. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs nine times, all in nine verses: seven occurrences are in Genesis and two are in Isaiah. Its earliest recorded use is in Genesis 44, and its latest is in Isaiah 51:22. The surrounding verse determines the particular role of the goblet in each passage, but the word itself denotes the vessel.

This adjective means “barley.” It describes something made from, containing, or associated with barley, rather than naming a person or action. Barley is a grain, so the word identifies the kind of grain involved when it modifies an object or substance. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears four times, in Numbers, Judges, 2 Kings, and Ezekiel. Its central meaning remains straightforward: it marks something as barley or barley-related; the surrounding verse determines the particular object being described.

“Laconian” is an adjective identifying something connected with Laconia or described by that regional name. In the Greek Old Testament, this word appears once, in Isaiah 3:22. Its basic role is descriptive: it marks a person, object, or feature as Laconian rather than naming an action or expressing an abstract quality. Because the available lexical meaning is brief and the verse text is not included here, the word’s precise force in Isaiah 3:22 must be understood from that passage’s surrounding context.

Loukam, also written Lukam, is a proper name. It identifies a specific named entity rather than describing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs once, at 1 Kings 4:12. Because the surrounding verse text is not included here, the name’s precise referent must be determined from that passage; the lexical evidence establishes the name itself, not additional details about the person or place it identifies.

Manōe, rendered Manoe, is a proper name referring to a man in the Greek Old Testament. It identifies the father of Samson in the book of Judges rather than describing a general quality, action, or object. The name appears 18 times across 14 verses, all within Judges. As a personal name, its meaning in a particular verse comes from the person being identified and the surrounding passage, not from an ordinary descriptive definition.

gl: retreat; place where one stays for the night
d: retreat; place where one stays for the night

e.t: This noun refers to a retreat or a place where someone stays for the night. It describes a location of shelter or lodging rather than an action or personal quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in 2 Kings 19:23. Its precise significance in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its ordinary sense is a place of withdrawal, rest, or overnight stay.

This verb means “hate”: to hold strong hostility or rejection toward someone or something. In the Greek Old Testament, it describes an opposing attitude rather than simple dislike, though its precise force depends on the surrounding sentence. The word appears 170 times across the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, showing that it is a commonly used expression for hostility or aversion. It can describe people who hate others, or a person’s rejection of a course, action, or object.

This noun means “adulterer”: a person who is unfaithful in marriage through a sexual relationship with someone who is not their spouse. It identifies the person who commits adultery, rather than the act itself. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs six times, including passages from Job, Psalms, Proverbs, Isaiah, Wisdom, and Sirach. Its precise force in any one verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This verb means to become weary through labor and to be sorely distressed. It describes the burden or exhaustion produced by difficult toil, rather than simply naming ordinary activity. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 33 times, with many occurrences in Ecclesiastes, where human labor is repeatedly considered in relation to its weariness and hardship. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea remains strenuous work that leaves a person troubled, worn, or distressed.

Mochorathi, also rendered Mokhorathi, is a proper name identifying a person. It is not presented here as a common word describing an action, quality, object, or relationship. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs once, at 1 Chronicles 11:36. Because no surrounding verse text is available here, the name’s particular identity and role must be determined from that passage’s context rather than from the name itself.

Nadabaios is a proper name, referring to a specific person rather than describing an action, quality, or spiritual concept. It is also represented as “Nathaveos,” giving two approved forms for the same named individual. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs once, at 1 Chronicles 5:19. The name by itself does not provide a broader definition; its precise significance depends on the person and surrounding passage identified in that verse.

This word means “graze”: to feed on grass or other vegetation, especially as an animal does in a pasture. It is a verb describing the act of grazing rather than the animal or the place where it feeds. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 20 times, including passages translated from the books of Genesis, Ezekiel, and Zephaniah. Its exact force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central meaning remains feeding by grazing.

This noun refers to levelling—the act or condition of being made level. It describes something brought down or evened out rather than left uneven. The word appears twice in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical writings preserved in the LXX, including one occurrence in Micah and one in Baruch. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse, but its central idea remains the making of a level surface or condition.

This Greek Old Testament noun means “armoury”: a place associated with storing weapons or military equipment. It names a location rather than an action, person, or quality. The word appears once in the Greek LXX, at 2 Chronicles 32:27. Because the lexical definition is brief and the surrounding verse text is not included here, the safest understanding is simply a place for weapons, with its exact force in that passage determined by context.

This Greek LXX adverb means “not yet.” It marks something that has not happened or is not true up to a particular point, while leaving open that it may happen later. In the LXX, it occurs once, in Exodus 9:30. Its exact force in that verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its basic function is to express an as-yet-unfulfilled condition or absent state.

This word means “always”. It is an adverb that describes something happening continually or at every time, rather than only once or occasionally. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears twice, both times in the book of Wisdom, showing a consistent sense across its uses. Its exact force in either passage is shaped by the surrounding sentence, but the central idea remains steady: an action, condition, or description that continues without interruption. The word occurs in Wisdom 11:21 and Wisdom 19:18. [p03:word:lxx:L709987:identity] [p03:word:lxx:L709987:occurrences] [p01:word:lxx:L709987:reference:0] [p01:word:lxx:L709987:reference:1]

This word means “lawlessness”: conduct that rejects or violates what is lawful. As a noun, it names the condition or practice of living without regard for law. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs seven times, including passages in Psalms, Proverbs, and 4 Maccabees. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage, but its central idea remains disregard for law rather than faithful obedience.

This noun refers to a pirate’s band—a group of pirates acting together. It names such a band rather than describing an individual pirate or a particular action. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs five times, appearing in Genesis, Job, and Psalms. Its precise force in any one passage depends on the surrounding verse, but its central meaning remains a pirate group or raiding company.

This word means “in violent rage; passionately.” It is an adverb, so it describes the manner in which someone acts or speaks—with intense, uncontrolled feeling rather than calm restraint. The sense can point either to fierce anger or to passionate intensity, depending on the sentence in which it appears. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, at 4 Maccabees 8:2. The reference identifies its location, while the surrounding verse is needed to determine exactly how that force is expressed there.

This adjective means “bitter.” It can describe a sharply unpleasant taste and, in biblical usage, may characterize something deeply painful or distressing. The word appears 34 times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented in this LXX corpus, showing that it is used across many passages rather than being limited to one setting. Its precise force in any verse depends on whether it describes a taste, an experience, or another quality presented as bitter.

e.h: A Brothel or House of Ill-Fame
e.t: This noun refers to a “house of ill-fame” or “brothel,” a place associated with prostitution. It names a physical establishment rather than a person, action, or moral quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, both times in Ezekiel 16, so its normal lexical sense is narrowly focused and does not represent a broad range of meanings. The exact force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and context.

This Greek LXX noun means “delegation”: a group or appointed representation sent to speak or act on behalf of others. It identifies a representative mission rather than an individual messenger. The word occurs twice in the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, once in Genesis and once in 2 Maccabees. Its exact force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and the people being represented.

This noun refers to an outer defensive work—a fortified barrier or bulwark built to protect a city or position. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears three times, in Jeremiah and Ezekiel, and its use concerns physical defenses around a city or defended place. The word points specifically to a structure placed outside or along a protected area, rather than to the people defending it. Its precise significance in any individual verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This verb means “build beside” or “credit.” It can describe adding a structure alongside something already present, and it can also express assigning something to a person’s account or recognition. In the Greek LXX, it occurs once, in Sirach 3:14. Because the verse text and surrounding context are not included here, the precise sense in that passage cannot be determined beyond these stated meanings.

e.h: A Greek Verb for Calling To
e.t: This verb means to “call to,” describing direct speech addressed toward someone. It presents the act of calling a person rather than merely speaking about that person. In the Greek Old Testament (the LXX) represented here, it occurs once, in 2 Maccabees 15:15. That reference shows where the word appears, while the surrounding verse is needed to determine the precise force of the call in context. Its central idea is a direct, personal address.

This verb means “motivate”: to move or encourage someone toward action. It describes the act of stirring another person’s will so that they are ready to do something, rather than merely informing them or expressing an idea. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs five times, chiefly in 4 Maccabees, and its precise force in any particular passage depends on the surrounding sentence and situation.

Sauē, also rendered Sai, is a proper name referring to a person in the Greek Old Testament. It is not a common word describing an action, quality, or object, but a personal designation. The name occurs twice in the Greek LXX, both times in Genesis 14, at Genesis 14:5 and Genesis 14:17. Without the surrounding verse text, the name itself does not provide further meaning beyond identifying the person to whom it refers.

Seph, also rendered Sef, is a proper name—the personal name of an individual rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament (the Septuagint), this name occurs once, at 2 Samuel 21:18. The name itself identifies the person, while the surrounding verse and passage are needed to explain that person’s role in the account. It should therefore be understood as a name, not expanded into an additional meaning or description.

This Greek LXX noun means “cheek,” the flesh on either side of the face. It identifies a person’s cheek as a physical body part, without itself expressing an action, emotion, or spiritual idea. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Deuteronomy 18:3. Its precise role in that verse depends on the surrounding passage and the way the body part is mentioned there.

e.h: A Lookout Place or Mountain Peak
e.t: This Greek LXX noun refers to a lookout place or a mountain peak—a raised location from which a person can observe the surrounding area. It can describe a physical high point, whether used for watching or simply identified by its elevation. The word occurs 11 times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek scriptural writings, including passages in Numbers, Judges, Kings, Chronicles, Isaiah, and Sirach. Its precise emphasis in any particular verse depends on whether the surrounding passage highlights the place as a vantage point or as a summit.

This adverb describes someone acting sullenly—showing a gloomy, displeased, or withdrawn manner. It tells how a person speaks or behaves rather than naming the person or action itself. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 3 Maccabees 5:34. The surrounding verse is needed to explain the specific situation, but the word itself points to an outward manner marked by displeasure or a darkened mood.

This LXX Greek verb means “make wise” or “sophisticated.” It describes giving someone wisdom, skill, or refined understanding rather than merely possessing knowledge. As a verb, it expresses an action that causes a person to become wise or capable. It occurs 21 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical writings, including Psalms, Proverbs, Ecclesiastes, and Sirach. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding context. The word appears in both ordinary descriptions of becoming capable and statements about wisdom’s value.

This verb means “bear down together”: it describes a combined downward force or movement, with multiple participants acting together rather than separately. It is a rare word in the Greek Old Testament, occurring once, in Isaiah 30:30. Its central idea is coordinated pressure or descent. The surrounding verse context would be needed to determine exactly what is bearing down and how this action functions there.

This word describes someone who is “fighting along with” another or is “allied with” them. As a noun, it can refer to an ally or fellow fighter; as an adjective, it describes an allied person or party. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs 13 times, chiefly in 1 and 2 Maccabees. Its central idea is cooperation in conflict or a shared military alliance, while the exact sense in a particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence.

This Greek LXX verb means “enter with”: it describes going into a place together with another person or group. The word focuses on shared entrance, rather than simply entering alone. It occurs five times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, including Exodus, Esther, Job, Sirach, and 1 Maccabees. Its exact force in any verse depends on who is entering and with whom, but its central idea remains accompanying someone into a place.

This verb means “destroy all at once,” describing complete destruction carried out in a single act rather than gradually or piece by piece. It is a forceful action word, presenting the destruction as comprehensive and immediate. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in Wisdom 11:19. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning remains the sudden, total destruction of what is being acted upon.

This verb means “wrap up”: it describes bringing something to a close or completing it. As an action word, it focuses on the act of drawing something together toward an ending rather than on a person, object, or quality. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs six times, appearing in Judges and in several later biblical writings, including Sirach and Maccabees. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

Sōsim, also rendered Sosim, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a particular person or place in the Greek Old Testament tradition, but the available lexical information does not specify which. The name occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, at 1 Chronicles 4:31. Its precise referent must therefore be identified from that passage and its surrounding genealogy, not from the name itself.

This noun means “nursing,” referring to the act or period of feeding a baby at the breast. It describes a stage associated with caring for and nourishing an infant, rather than a person who performs that care. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, in 4 Maccabees 16:7. The surrounding verse text is not available here, so the word’s precise emphasis in that passage cannot be stated beyond its basic meaning. Its central idea remains the nourishment of an infant through nursing.

This adjective means “rough.” It describes something with an uneven, harsh, or irregular quality rather than a smooth one. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it appears six times, including descriptions connected with roads, land, or other things whose surface or character is not gentle or even. Its exact force depends on the noun and sentence where it appears, but the central idea remains a lack of smoothness or softness. The word occurs in both Old Testament and deuterocanonical passages in this Greek corpus.

This word means “path” or “track,” referring to a route or course that can be followed. As an adjective, it describes something connected with a path or track rather than naming a person or object by itself. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs three times, all in Proverbs, where the surrounding wording determines the precise sense in each passage. Its basic idea remains a defined route or direction of travel.

“Proudly” describes doing something with an attitude of self-importance, superiority, or open arrogance. As an adverb, it tells how someone speaks, acts, or carries out an action. This LXX word appears three times, all in the deuterocanonical books of 1 and 2 Maccabees. Its precise force in any particular sentence depends on the surrounding words, but its central sense is clear: acting in a boastful or haughty manner rather than with humility.

This noun means “baldness” or “bald head,” referring to the condition or appearance of having little or no hair on the head. In the Greek Old Testament, it is used for a visible physical condition and can describe the head itself. It occurs ten times across nine Old Testament verses, especially in Leviticus and Isaiah. Its exact force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding wording and context.

This noun means “loving one's fellow-citizens”: it describes a person who cares about and shows loyalty toward the people of the same city or civic community. The word appears once in the Greek Old Testament corpus, in 2 Maccabees 14:37. That single occurrence identifies the word’s basic social meaning, but the verse text is needed to explain the particular force it has in that passage. It refers to a person characterized by fellow-citizen love, rather than naming a place, event, or action.

This noun refers to “looking out” or a “watch”—the act or duty of keeping watch. It describes attentive observation rather than a person who watches. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek Jewish writings, it occurs 12 times, including passages in 2 Samuel, 1 Chronicles, 1 Maccabees, and 2 Maccabees. Its precise force in any verse depends on whether the surrounding passage presents a period of watchfulness or the act of looking out.

This Greek LXX noun means “joyfulness” or “delight”—a glad, pleasurable state of heart. It names an experience of happiness rather than an action, command, or person. The word occurs twice in the Greek Old Testament, appearing once in 1 Samuel and once in Jeremiah. Its precise emphasis in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but its central sense remains gladness and delight. Scripture uses this word rarely, so its basic meaning is more important than any broad range of repeated uses.

This word refers to cherubim, heavenly beings associated with God’s presence. It is a noun and normally names these beings rather than describing a human quality or action. In the Greek Old Testament, the word appears 83 times, chiefly in passages concerning the tabernacle, temple, worship, and prophetic visions. Its first listed occurrence is Genesis 3:24, and it continues through descriptions of sacred furnishings and heavenly scenes. The word identifies a distinct class of beings; the surrounding passage determines what they are doing or portraying in a particular verse.

Chober, also rendered Khover, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a particular person in the Greek Old Testament, and its precise significance comes from the surrounding passage rather than from a general abstract meaning. This name occurs once in the Greek LXX, at Numbers 26:29. The form Chober is the established English rendering associated with this individual name.

This Greek LXX noun refers to money or financial resources—what a person receives as proceeds or keeps as a fund. It can describe available wealth rather than a particular object, so the surrounding sentence shows whether the emphasis is on income, stored money, or financial means. The word occurs 41 times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, with especially frequent use in Sirach and 2 Maccabees. Its central idea remains money regarded as something gained, possessed, or available for use.

gl: sing psalms; sing to the harp
d: sing psalms; sing to the harp

e.t: This verb means “sing psalms” or “sing to the harp.” It describes making musical praise, specifically with psalm singing or harp accompaniment. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at 2 Chronicles 5:13. The word therefore points to musical worship expressed through singing and instrumental music, while the exact force of its use in that verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This word refers to roaring: a loud, forceful sound. It is a noun, so it names the sound rather than describing an action or person. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Ezekiel 19:7. Its basic meaning remains focused on the audible quality of a roar, while the surrounding verse determines what is producing the sound and how the word functions in that particular passage.
